en: The Nṛsiṃhatāpinī Upaniṣad
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all things, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with his uninjured wheel-rims grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
The First Upaniṣad

Om. This was indeed water, a mere ocean. Prajāpati alone came into being upon a lotus leaf. Within his mind, desire arose: "May I procreate this. Therefore, what a person first conceives in the mind, that he speaks with speech and performs through action. Regarding this, it has been said: "In the beginning, desire arose within the mind as the first seed of being. The seers, searching in their hearts with wisdom, discovered the bond of existence in non-existence. Whatever one desires comes to pass for him who knows this. 1.1.1.10–12.13.10 (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.1–5) Om. This was indeed water, a mere ocean. Prajāpati alone came into being upon a lotus leaf. Within his mind, desire arose:

He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he beheld this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter; by means of it, indeed, he created all this, whatever exists here. Therefore, they say that all this, whatever exists here, is Ānuṣṭubha. From the Anuṣṭubh, indeed, these beings are born; through the Anuṣṭubh, once born, they live.

They enter into the *anuṣṭubh* as they depart; this [verse] belongs to it. The *anuṣṭubh* is first, the *anuṣṭubh* is last. The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech; by means of speech they depart, and by means of speech they rise up. This *anuṣṭubh* is the supreme among the meters. Thus [it is said]. 2.

One should know that the earth, together with its oceans, mountains, and seven continents, is the first foot of that Sāman. One should know that the intermediate space, frequented by hosts of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases, is the second foot of that Sāman. One should know that heaven, frequented by all the gods—the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—is the third foot of that Sāman. One should know that the supreme, stainless ether, which is the very nature of Brahman, is the fourth foot of that Sāman. He who knows this attains immortality. || 3 ||
The four Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan—along with their auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) and branches (śākhās), constitute the four feet. || 4 ||
What is the meditation? What is the deity? What are the limbs? What are the deities of those limbs? What is the meter? Who is the seer? || 5 ||

Prajāpati said: "He who knows that eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitrī which is consecrated by glory (*śrī*), and which is a limb (*aṅga*) of the Sāman—he is indeed consecrated with glory. All the Vedas begin with the *praṇava*; he who knows that *praṇava*, which is a limb of the Sāman, conquers the three worlds. The twenty-four-syllabled Mahālakṣmī is a *yajus*; he who knows it as a limb of the Sāman becomes possessed of long life, fame, renown, knowledge, and sovereignty.
Therefore, one should know this Sāman together with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality. || 6 ||

They do not permit women or Śūdras to know the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, the Yajurlakṣmī, or the thirty-two-syllable Sāman; he who knows these attains immortality. If a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, the Yajus, and the Praṇava, he goes to the lower regions after death; therefore, one should never teach them. If one teaches them, that teacher, by that very act, goes to the lower regions after death. || 7 ||

Prajāpati said: "Agni indeed is the gods; he is all this, all beings, the vital breaths, the senses, cattle, food, the unmanifested, the sovereign ruler (samrāṭ), the self-ruler (svarāṭ), and the wide-ruler (virāṭ). One should know him as the first foot of the Sāman. The Sun, who consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas—the golden person within the sun—one should know him as the second foot of the Sāman. He who is the lord of the plants, the moon, the sovereign of the stars—one should know him as the third foot of the Sāman."
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra; he is the imperishable, supreme self-ruler. One should know that fourth foot of the Sāman; he who knows it attains immortality. || 8 ||

One should know the *ugra* as the first beginning, the *jvalat* as the second beginning, the *nṛsiṃha* as the third beginning, and the *mṛtyu* as the fourth beginning of the Sāman; he who knows this attains immortality. Therefore, one does not recite this Sāman anywhere unless it is for the purpose of giving it; if one desires to give it, one may give it to a son who is obedient or to another disciple. || 9 ||

One should know the Sāman as Him who reclines upon the ocean of milk, who has the form of a man-lion, who is the object of meditation for yogis, and the supreme state; he who knows this attains immortality. || 10 ||

One should know the *vīra* as the first syllable of the first *ardhya*, that same [syllable] as the last of the second, *haṃ* as the last of the third, and *bhī* as the last of the fourth; one should know this *sāman*. Whoever knows it attains immortality. Therefore, whoever knows this *sāman* through the mouth of any teacher whatsoever is liberated from *saṃsāra* by that very body; he liberates others and becomes one who desires liberation.

Through recitation (*japa*), one attains the vision of the deity with that very body; therefore, this alone is the primary gateway in the Kali age, and not others. Consequently, one should know this *Sāman* together with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality. || 11 ||

He is the Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), the Truth (*satya*), the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, whose seed is drawn upward, the three-eyed one, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita. He is the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Creatures, the wielder of the Pināka bow, indeed of immeasurable splendor. He is the Sovereign of all sciences, the Lord of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the Veda; he who truly knows you, who are expressed by the Yajurveda as Sāman, attains immortality—he who knows this, goes to the state of the deathless. || 12 ||

One should know that the first part of the first *mahāprathama* [quarter], the first part of the second [quarter] ending in the accusative, the first part of the third [quarter] ending in the instrumental, and the first part of the fourth [quarter] ending in the dative, constitute the *sāman*. He who knows this attains immortality. Therefore, this *sāman* is the Supreme Brahman, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandamaya*). One who knows it thus becomes immortal even here. Therefore, one should know this *sāman* with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality. 13.

By this indeed the creators of the universe (Viśvasṛjs) created this entire universe; because they created the universe, they are called Viśvasṛjs. After them, the entire universe is born. They attain the same world as Brahman, the same power, and union with him. Therefore, one should know this Sāman together with its limbs; he who knows it attains immortality. || 14 ||

One should know Viṣṇu as the last letter of the first [word], Mukha as the last letter of the second, Bhadra as the last letter of the third, and Myaha as the last letter of the fourth; he who knows this Sāman attains immortality. He who knows that which is this "whatever exists" within the Self, as the Anuṣṭubh within Brahman—he who knows it attains immortality. To him who desires to remain right here, he grants sovereignty over all things.
Wherever he may die, at the end of the body, the Divine One teaches him the supreme Brahman, the Savior (Tāraka), by which he becomes immortal and attains immortality. 15.

Therefore, one mutters this which is situated in the midst of the Sāman; therefore, this is a limb of the Sāman; therefore, this is a limb of the Sāman belonging to Prajāpati. "He who knows thus"—this is the Great Upaniṣad. He who knows this Great Upaniṣad becomes Mahāviṣṇu, having performed the preparatory rites; he becomes Mahāviṣṇu. 16.
The Second Upanishad

The gods, indeed, were afraid of death, of evil, and of saṃsāra; they approached Prajāpati, and he bestowed upon them this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter. By means of it, they conquered death, crossed over evil, and crossed over saṃsāra. Therefore, whoever fears death, evil, and saṃsāra should receive this King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter. He crosses over death, he crosses over evil, and he crosses over saṃsāra. || 1 ||

Of that *praṇava*, the first *mātrā* is the earth, the syllable *a*; it consists of the *ṛc*s, the *Ṛgveda*, Brahmā, the Vasus, the *Gāyatrī* meter, and the *Gārhapatya* fire; it constitutes the first foot of the *Sāman*. The second [mātrā] is the intermediate space, the syllable *u*; it consists of the *yajus*s, the *Yajurveda*, Viṣṇu, the Rudras, the *Triṣṭubh* meter, and the *Dakṣiṇāgni* fire; it constitutes the second foot of the *Sāman*.

The third heaven is that *makāra*; it consists of the Sāmans, the Sāmaveda, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Jagatī meter, and the Āhavanīya fire. This is the third foot of the Sāman. That half-mora at its conclusion is the world of Soma; it is the syllable *Oṃ*, consisting of the Atharvan mantras, the Atharvaveda, the Saṃvartaka fire, the Maruts, the Virāj meter, and Ekārṣi; it is remembered as the radiant one. This is the fourth foot of the Sāman. || 2 ||

The first foot consists of eight syllables, and there are three feet of eight syllables each; thus, thirty-two syllables are obtained. The Anuṣṭubh indeed consists of thirty-two syllables. By means of the Anuṣṭubh all this was created, and by means of the Anuṣṭubh all this is withdrawn. || 3 ||

This [mantra] has five limbs. There are four feet; there are four limbs; everything together with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) constitutes the fifth. [The limbs are]: "Homage to the heart (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*); *svāhā* to the head (*śirase*); *vaṣaṭ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhāyai*); *huṃ* to the armor (*kavacāya*); *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astrāya*). He interweaves them: the first with the first, the second with the second, the third with the third, the fourth with the fourth, and the fifth with the fifth. Indeed, these worlds are interwoven; therefore, the limbs are interwoven. || 4 ||
"This syllable 'Om' is all this; therefore, the syllable 'Om' occurs before and after every syllable. Those who discourse on Brahman teach the placement of the syllables. || 5 ||

One should indeed know his fierce first station; he who knows it attains immortality. The second station is Vīra; the third station is Mahāviṣṇu; the fourth station is Jvalant; the fifth station is Sarvatomukha; the sixth station is Nṛsiṃha; the seventh station is Bhīṣaṇa; the eighth station is Bhadra; the ninth station is Mṛtyumṛtyu; the tenth station is Namāmi; one should know the eleventh station as Aham. He who knows it attains immortality. || 6 ||

Or the *anuṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables; by means of the *anuṣṭubh*, all this was created, and by means of the *anuṣṭubh*, all this is withdrawn. Therefore, one should know that everything is the *anuṣṭubh*; he who knows this attains immortality. || 7 ||

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "Now, why is it called *ugram* (the Fierce)? He, Prajāpati, replied: "Because by its own majesty it seizes up (*ud-gṛhṇāti*) all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings; it creates incessantly, emits, and causes them to dwell; it is seized up and is grasped. 'Praise the renowned one, who sits upon the chariot-seat, the youthful, fierce one, like a terrifying beast, the slayer. 'Be gracious to the singer, O Rudra; being praised, let thy missiles pass us by. Therefore it is called *ugram*. || 8 ||

Now, why is he called *vīra*? Because by his own majesty he causes all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings to cease, to cause to cease, and incessantly creates, emits, and abides within them. Since from him is born one who is heroic, skillful in action, beautiful to behold, diligent with the pressing-stones, and desirous of the gods—for these reasons he is called *vīra*. || 9 ||

Now, why is he called Mahāviṣṇu? Because by his own majesty he pervades and causes all the worlds, all the gods, all selves, and all beings to be pervaded—just as oil pervades and permeates a ball of meat, being spread across it, woven through it, and interwoven with it from its very root. Because there is no other born superior to him, who has entered into all worlds;
Prajāpati, in harmony with his progeny, attends to the three lights and the sixteenth—that is why he is called Mahāviṣṇu. || 10 ||

Now, why is it said "the blazing"? Because by its own majesty it blazes, causes to blaze, is blazed over, and causes to be blazed over all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings with its own splendor. It is the progenitor, the impeller, the radiant, the illuminating, the shining, the blazing, the blazer, the heating, the heater, the scorching, the luminous, the shining, the beautiful, the beautifying, the auspicious; therefore it is called "the blazing. || 11 ||

Now, why is it called "all-facing" (*sarvatomukha*)? Because by its own majesty, although itself devoid of sense organs, it sees all worlds, all gods, all selves, and all beings from every side; it hears from every side, it moves from every side, it grasps from every side; it is omnipresent and stands pervading everything. "The One who was here at the beginning, from whom this world arose, the guardian of the universe—to Him the world returns at the time of the final transition, Him I bow down to, the All-facing. Therefore, it is called "all-facing. || 12 ||

Now, why is he called *Nṛsiṃha*? Because among all beings, man (*nṛ*) is the most powerful and the most excellent, and the lion (*siṃha*) is the most powerful and the most excellent; therefore, the Supreme Lord became *Nṛsiṃha*. Indeed, this form which is imperishable is for the welfare of the world. "For that heroic power Viṣṇu is praised; like a terrifying beast, roaming on the mountains, whose three wide strides encompass all worlds. Therefore, he is called *Nṛsiṃha*. 13.

Now, why is it called "Bhīṣaṇam" (the Terrifying)? Because its form is terrifying; upon seeing it, all worlds, all gods, and all beings flee in fear, yet it itself does not fear from any quarter whatsoever. As it is said: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear of Him the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni, Indra, and Death run as the fifth"—therefore it is called "Bhīṣaṇam. || 14 ||

Now, why is it called "Bhadram" (the auspicious)? Because, having become auspicious oneself, one always bestows what is auspicious. It is radiant, shining, beautiful, gleaming, and excellent. "O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones worthy of sacrifice, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain that lifespan ordained by the gods. Therefore, it is called "Bhadram. 15.

Now, why is he called "Death-of-Death"? Because by his own majesty, as soon as he is remembered, he slays both death and premature death for his devotees. He who is the giver of self and the giver of strength, whose command the entire universe and the gods obey; whose shadow is immortality, and who is the Death-of-Death—to that God let us do worship with an oblation. Therefore, he is called "Death-of-Death. (16)

Now, why is it said, "I bow"? Because all the gods, those seeking liberation, and the exponents of Brahman bow to him. "Brahmaṇaspati now indeed utters the praiseworthy mantra, in which Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and the gods have made their abodes. Therefore it is said, "I bow. || 17 ||

Now, why is it said, "I"? "I am the first-born of Truth (Ṛta), prior to the gods, the navel of immortality. He who gives me, he indeed possesses the gods. I am the food; I eat the eater of food. I have surpassed the entire world. He who knows this [possesses] the light of heaven"—thus ends the Mahopaniṣad. 4.
The Third Upanishad
The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, tell us the power (śakti) and the seed-syllable (bīja) of this Nārasiṃha king of mantras, which is based on the Anuṣṭubh meter. || 1 ||

Prajāpati said: "This is indeed the Nārasiṃhī Māyā; she creates all this, she protects all this, and she withdraws all this. Therefore, one should know this power as Māyā. He who knows this power, this Māyā, crosses over evil, he crosses over death, he crosses over saṃsāra, he attains immortality, and he enjoys great prosperity. || 2 ||

The exponents of Brahman deliberate upon this: whether it be short, long, or protracted. If it is short, it burns away all evil and one attains immortality; if it is long, one attains great prosperity and attains immortality; if it is protracted, one becomes possessed of knowledge and attains immortality. || 3 ||

This very point has been stated by the Seer as an illustration: "O you who possess the *ṛjīṣa*, the deliverer, protect her—Śrī, Lakṣmī, Aupalā, Ambikā, and the Cow; and that which they call the sixth, Indrasenā. To that Knowledge, the source of Brahman, who is of like form, I go for refuge for the sake of this life. || 4 ||

Space is the ultimate resort of all these beings; indeed, all these beings are born from space alone, and having been born from space alone, they live, and at their departure, they merge back into space. Therefore, one should know space as the seed.

This very point has been stated by the Seer as an illustration: "The Swan dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the intermediate space, the Hotṛ dwelling at the altar, the Guest dwelling in the house, the one dwelling among men, the one dwelling in the best, the one dwelling in truth, the one dwelling in the sky, born of the waters, born of the cows, born of truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth. "He who knows thus"—so says the Mahopaniṣad.
The Fourth Upanishad
The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, tell us the limb-mantras of this Nārasiṃha King of Mantras, which is based on the Anuṣṭubh meter."
Prajāpati said: "One should know the Praṇava, the Sāvitrī, the Yajurlakṣmī, and the Nṛsiṃhagāyatrī as the limbs; he who knows them attains immortality. || 2 ||

"Om"—this syllable is all this. Its further explanation is as follows: whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be—all that is indeed the syllable Om; and whatever else is beyond the three periods of time, that too is indeed the syllable Om. For all this is Brahman, and this Self is Brahman. This very Self has four quarters.
The first quarter is Vaiśvānara, whose sphere is the waking state, who is conscious of external objects, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences gross objects. || 4 ||
The second quarter is the Taijasa, whose sphere is the dream state, who is conscious of the internal, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences subtle objects. || 5 ||

That state where one who is asleep desires no desire and sees no dream—that is deep sleep (*suṣupta*). In this stage of deep sleep, he has become unified, a mass of consciousness, consisting of pure bliss, experiencing bliss, having the mind as his gateway; this is the Wise One (*prājña*), the third foot. He is the Lord of all, he is the All-knowing, he is the Inner Ruler, he is the source of all; for from him come the origin and dissolution of all beings. 6.

They consider the Fourth (the *turya*) to be neither inwardly cognitive, nor outwardly cognitive, nor cognitive of both, nor cognitive, nor non-cognitive, nor a mass of consciousness; unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without marks, unthinkable, indescribable, the essence of the realization of the oneness of the Self, the cessation of the phenomenal world, tranquil, auspicious, and non-dual; that is the Self, that is to be known. 7.

Now, Sāvitrī is declared by means of the Gāyatrī metre and the Yajus formula; by her all this is pervaded: "ghṛṇi" consists of two syllables, "sūrya" consists of three, and "āditya" consists of three. This indeed is the eight-syllabled foot of Sāvitra, consecrated with glory; he who knows thus is indeed consecrated with glory. 8.

This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "In the imperishable syllable, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled; he who does not know that—what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they sit together here. (9)
"Indeed, there is no need for Ṛg, Yajus, or Sāman for him who knows the Sāvitra," so it is said.
"Oṃ bhūrlakṣmīḥ, bhuvarlakṣmīḥ, svarlakṣmīḥ, kālakarṇī; may that Mahālakṣmī inspire us. This indeed is the Mahālakṣmī Yajur-gāyatrī, consisting of twenty-four syllables. || 11 ||
The Gāyatrī indeed is all this, whatever exists here; therefore, he who knows this Mahālakṣmī of the Yajurveda attains great prosperity. || 12 ||

"Oṃ, let us know Nṛsiṃha; let us meditate upon Him whose claws are like thunderbolts; may that Lion inspire us"—this indeed is the Nṛsiṃha-Gāyatrī, which is the source of the gods and the Vedas. Whoever knows this becomes possessed of a source. || 13 ||
The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "Now, by which mantras is the Lord praised so that He becomes pleased and reveals His own Self? Tell us that, O Blessed One. || 14 ||

Prajāpati said: "Om! Salutations again and again to that Lord who is indeed the divine Nṛsiṃha, and who is Brahmā—Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ. [Just as the beginning and end are stated in the first mantra, so they are to be understood in all mantras] ...and who is Viṣṇu... || 2 ||
.........and he who is Maheśvara......... || 3 ||
And whatever person... || 4 ||
.........and he who is Īśvara......... || 5 ||
...that which is Śrī... || 7 ||
......that which is the primordial nature (prakṛti)...... || 9 ||
......the knowledge that is [this]...... || 10 ||
......and that which is the syllable Oṃ...... || 11 ||
......the four half-mātrās...... || 12 ||
......those Vedas, together with their auxiliary sciences, their branches, and their histories...... || 13 ||
And those who [practice] the five fires... || 14 ||
......which are the seven great utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis)...... || 15 ||
......and those who are the eight guardians of the world (lokapālas)...... || 16 ||
......and those who are the eight Vasus...... || 17 ||
And those who are the eleven Rudras... || 18 ||
And those who are the twelve Ādityas... || 19 ||
And those eight planets... || 20 ||
And those which are the five great elements (pañcamahābhūta) ... || 21 ||
.........and whatever time there may be......... || 22 ||
And whoever [is] Manu... || 23 ||
And that which is death... || 24 ||
And he who is Yama... || 25 ||
.........and he who is the Ender (Antaka)......... || 26 ||
.........and that which is the vital breath (prāṇa)......... || 27 ||
And he who is the Sun... || 28 ||
And that which is Soma... || 29 ||
......and that which is the Virāt Puruṣa...... || 30 ||
And whatever living being... || 31 ||
"...and that which is all... || 32 || Thus, [there are] thirty-two. Prajāpati said to them: "With these mantras, you should constantly praise the God. || 15 ||

Then the God becomes pleased and reveals His own self; therefore, he who constantly praises the God with these mantras beholds the God and attains immortality—he who knows thus, this is the Great Upaniṣad. 16.
The Fifth Upanishad

The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, teach us the wheel named Mahācakra belonging to the Nārasiṃha King of Mantras, which is of the Anuṣṭubh meter; they instruct the diligent seeker that it fulfills all desires and is the door to liberation. || 1 ||

Prajāpati said: "This Great Cakra, the Sudarśana, consists of six syllables; therefore it has six spokes and it is a wheel with six petals. There are indeed six seasons; thus it is commensurate with the seasons. In the center there is a hub (nābhi); upon the hub these spokes are established. By means of Māyā all this is encircled; yet Māyā does not touch the Self (Ātman). Therefore, it is encircled by Māyā on the outside. || 2 ||

Then there is an eight-spoked, eight-petaled wheel; for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and it is commensurate with the Gāyatrī. It is surrounded by an outer illusion (māyā); for this constitutes field after field, indeed, as that very illusion. || 3 ||

Now, there is a wheel with twelve spokes and twelve petals; for the Jagatī meter consists of twelve syllables, and it is commensurate with the Jagatī. It is encircled on the outside by the Māyā-thread. || 4 ||

Now, there is a wheel with sixteen spokes and sixteen petals; for the person (puruṣa) consists of sixteen parts, and all this is indeed the person; it is measured by the person and is externally enveloped by illusion (māyā). || 5 ||

Now, there is a wheel with thirty-two spokes and thirty-two petals; for the *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables, and by means of the *anuṣṭubh*, all this comes into being. It is surrounded on the outside by *māyā*. || 6 ||
This [chariot] is indeed well-fastened by the spokes; these Vedas are the spokes. It moves all around by means of the leaves; the meters are indeed the leaves. || 7 ||

This is the great Sudarśana-cakra. In its center, at the hub, is the single-syllabled Nārasiṃha, which is the saving (tāraka) syllable. On the six petals, there is the six-syllabled Sudarśana; on the eight petals, the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa; and on the twelve petals, the twelve-syllabled Vāsudeva. On the sixteen petals are the sixteen vowels beginning with *mātṛkā*, accompanied by the nasal bindu.

Upon the thirty-two petals is the thirty-two-syllable King of Mantras, the Nārasiṃha, in the Anuṣṭubh meter. This very discus named Sudarśana is the fulfiller of all desires, the door to liberation, consisting of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Brahman, and the nectar of immortality. The Vasus sit to its east, the Rudras to the south, the Ādityas to the west, and the Viśvedevas to the north; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are in the nave, while the sun and the moon are on the two sides.

This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "In the imperishable syllable, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled; he who does not know that—what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they have attained union. (9)

Whoever, whether a child or a youth, knows this Great Sudarśana Cakra becomes great; he becomes a teacher and an instructor of all mantras. One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the Anuṣṭubh meter and perform the worship with the Anuṣṭubh meter. This [mantra] is a destroyer of demons and a deliverer from death; having received it from the Guru, one should bind it around the neck, the arm, or the tuft of hair. The earth with its seven islands is not sufficient as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); therefore, whatever cow one gives with faith, that becomes the sacrificial fee. || 10 ||
The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, tell us the fruit of this Nārasiṃha King of Mantras, which is in the Anuṣṭubh meter. || 11 ||

Prajāpati said: "He who constantly studies this Nārasiṃha King of Mantras in the Anuṣṭubh meter becomes purified by Agni; he becomes purified by Vāyu; he becomes purified by Āditya; he becomes purified by Soma; he becomes purified by Satya; he becomes purified by Brahmā; he becomes purified by Viṣṇu; he becomes purified by Rudra; he becomes purified by the gods; he becomes purified by all. He becomes purified by all, he becomes purified by all. || 12 ||

He who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter—he crosses over death; he crosses over evil; he crosses over the killing of a Brahmin; he crosses over the killing of an embryo; he crosses over the killing of a hero; he crosses over the killing of all; he crosses over saṃsāra; he crosses over everything; he crosses over everything. 13.

He who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, paralyzes fire; he paralyzes wind; he paralyzes the sun; he paralyzes the *stoma*; he paralyzes water; he paralyzes all the gods; he paralyzes all the *grahas*; he paralyzes poison; he paralyzes poison. || 14 ||

Whoever constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, he attracts the gods; he attracts the yakṣas; he attracts the nāgas; he attracts the grahas; he attracts human beings; he attracts everyone; he attracts everyone. 15.

He who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter, conquers the Bhūrloka; he conquers the Bhuvarloka; he conquers the Svarloka; he conquers the Maharloka; he conquers the Janoloka; he conquers the Tapoloka; he conquers the Satyaloka; he conquers all the worlds; he conquers all the worlds. 16.

Whoever constantly studies this *Anuṣṭubh* king of mantras, he sacrifices with the *Agniṣṭoma*; he sacrifices with the *Ukthya*; he sacrifices with the *Ṣoḍaśin*; he sacrifices with the *Vājapeya*; he sacrifices with the *Atirātra*; he sacrifices with the *Aptoryāma*; he sacrifices with the *Aśvamedha*; he sacrifices with all the sacrificial rites; he sacrifices with all the sacrificial rites. || 17 ||

He who constantly studies this king of mantras, the Nārasiṃha in the Anuṣṭubh meter—he studies the Ṛgveda; he studies the Yajurveda; he studies the Sāmaveda; he studies the Atharvaveda; he studies the Aṅgirasas; he studies the Vedic branches (śākhās); he studies the Purāṇas; he studies the Kalpas; he studies the Gāthās; he studies the Nārāśaṃsīs; he studies the Praṇava. He who studies the Praṇava studies everything; he studies everything. 18.

One hundred uninitiated [students] are equal to one initiated [student]; one hundred initiated students are equal to one householder; one hundred householders are equal to one forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); one hundred forest-dwellers are equal to one ascetic (*yati*); a full hundred ascetics are equal to one reciter of the *Rudra*; one hundred reciters of the *Rudra* are equal to one teacher of the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā*; and one hundred teachers of the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā* are equal to one [teacher of the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śikhā*].
One teacher of the Tāpanīya Upaniṣad is equal to a hundred teachers of the Tāpanīya Upaniṣad; one teacher of the King of Mantras is equal to that [hundred]. || 19 ||

This indeed is the supreme abode of the teacher of the King of Mantras, where the sun does not shine, where the wind does not blow, where the moon does not gleam, where the stars do not shine, where fire does not burn, and where death does not enter; it is ever-blissful, supreme bliss, peaceful, eternal, the ever-auspicious Brahman, worshipped by Brahmā and others, the supreme state to be meditated upon by yogis, having gone to which yogis do not return. 20.

This very thing is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky. The inspired poets, ever-watchful and praising, kindle that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. This belongs to one who is free from desire; this belongs to one who is free from desire—he who knows thus. Thus ends the Mahopaniṣad. 21.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with uninjured wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Thus ends the Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad.
